newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thai stocks seen up on technical rebound, rates.
newsitem.headline: Thai stocks seen up on technical rebound, rates.

text.p: The battered Thai stock market, which has plunged to its lowest levels in more than six years, could rise slightly this week on hopes that banks will cut interest rates, analysts said.
They said there were signs that the government would ask state-controlled Krung Thai Bank Plc, Thailand's second-largest commercial bank, to cut its lending rate by 25 basis points later this month.
Thai interest rates, at a minimum of 12.75 percent, are among the highest in Southeast Asia.

Krung Thai Bank and a number of leading commercial banks late last month cut their minimum lending rates by 25 basis points but the moves failed to boost market sentiment. Investors felt the cut was too small to stimulate the country's flagging economy.

"Other major Thai banks are expected to follow Krung Thai if it cuts its lending rates. Although the cut isn't much, it will help boost market sentiment which was shaken badly due to heavy selling by foreigners of large capitalised stocks last week," said Thanadech Mahapokai of Book Club Finance and Securities.
Analysts said the market should advance partly on a technical rebound after falling 8.3 percent last week.

"Investors believe that current strong psychological supporting level is at 600 points and I guess that the market would see a minimal technical rebound," said Thanawat Patchimkul of Seamico Securities.
The SET index on Friday closed 8.63 points lower at 605.43. It was the lowest close since January 7, 1991, when the index finished at 595.36. At its peak in February 1996 the index edged past 1,400.

One central concern for months has been the exposure of finance houses to bad loans to the ailing property sector. The market is watching closely to see whether a planned merger between troubled finance company Finance One Plc and Thai Danu Bank Plc goes through as planned.

Worries over the merger, compounded by concern over first-quarter corporate results and exports, persuaded foreign investors to unload large capitalised issues in bank, finance, communications, energy and property last week, analysts said.

"The problem with the market right now is that foreign investors have lost their confidence in the Thai economy. The outlook for the economy is dim and it's difficult to recover even in the next one or two years," said Thanawat.
Private economists project Thailand's economic growth will slow to about five percent this year -- its lowest level since 1986 -- compared with 6.7 percent in 1996.
Meanwhile on the exports front, economists feel the Bank of Thailand's 1997 target of 7.7 percent growth may be optimistic.

On the continuing merger talks between Thailand's largest finance company, Finance One, and the medium-sized Thai Danu Bank, analysts said if the deal succeeded it would help the prospects of several planned mergers among finance companies.
A senior executive of Thai Danu Bank said last week that the boards of the two firms were scheduled to hold meetings on May 15 to approve the merger after due diligence was completed.
The market has been awash with talk that due diligence will expose Finance One's weak financial position and shareholders may not approve the merger.
